[Data Science]{.blue} ::: {.my-grey} [{{< meta semester >}} | {{< meta course >}}]{}
[Jeffrey M. Girard | Lecture {{< meta lecture >}}]{} ::: ![](../../img/proud_coder_357EDD.svg){.absolute bottom=30 right=0 width="400"} ::: ## Roadmap ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="60%"} - Understand the difference between character strings and factors - Control the order of categorical data in plots and tables - Recode, collapse, and "lump" factor levels to simplify messy data ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv4 width="40%"} {{< lif "../../icons/map.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ::: # Creating Factors ## What are Factors? {.fs70} ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="60%"} - **Question:** *Why not just use strings for categories?* - [Factors]{.b .blue} are used for categorical variables with a fixed and known set of possible values (***levels***) - Each level can also have a nice display ***label*** - Unlike strings, factors allow you to control the ***order*** of categories and check for invalid values ::: {.fragment .mt1} - We use the {forcats} package (part of the {tidyverse}) to work with them - Most functions in this package start with `fct_` ::: ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv4 width="40%"} {{< lif "../../icons/theater.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ::: ## Creating Factors ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *How do we convert raw data into a factor?* ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Raw data as numbers (where 1=Female, 2=Male and 11 is a typo) sex <- c(2, 1, 1, 2, 11) ``` ::: :::{.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Convert to factor so R knows that only 1 and 2 were valid fct_sex <- factor(sex, levels = c(1, 2)) fct_sex ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 1 1 2 Levels: 1 2 ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Each level can be given a string to serve as its "label" factor(sex, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Female", "Male")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] Male Female Female Male Levels: Female Male ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Factors vs. Strings ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *What happens if we don't specify levels?* ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Raw data as strings birth_months <- c("Jan", "Feb", "Feb", "Jan", "Apr", "Mar", "Apr") # Default levels = observed values in alphanumeric order factor(birth_months) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] Jan Feb Feb Jan Apr Mar Apr Levels: Apr Feb Jan Mar ``` ::: ::: :::{.fragment} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Explicitly define levels and order (including unobserved ones) factor(birth_months, levels = c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] Jan Feb Feb Jan Apr Mar Apr Levels: Jan Feb Mar Apr May Jun Jul Aug Sep Oct Nov Dec ``` ::: ::: ::: ## A Safer Alternative ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *Are there better tools for creating factors than base R?* The {forcats} package provides `fct()`. It is safer than `factor()` because it errors if you include a value not in the levels, and it orders by first appearance. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Base R factor() silently creates NAs for typos factor(c("Dec", "Apr", "Jam", "Mar"), levels = c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "Dec")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] Dec Apr Mar Levels: Jan Feb Mar Apr Dec ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # forcats::fct() catches the error for us fct(c("Dec", "Apr", "Jam", "Mar"), levels = c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "Dec")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `fct()`: ! All values of `x` must appear in `levels` or `na` ℹ Missing level: "Jam" ``` ::: ::: # Ordering Levels ## Introducing the GSS Dataset ::: {.fs80} To explore reordering and modifying factors, we will use the `gss_cat` dataset. This is a sample of data from the General Social Survey. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) data("gss_cat", package = "forcats") glimpse(gss_cat) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 21,483 Columns: 9 $ year 2000, 2000, 2000, 2000, 2000, 2000, 2000, 2000, 2000, 2000, 20… $ marital Never married, Divorced, Widowed, Never married, Divorced, Mar… $ age 26, 48, 67, 39, 25, 25, 36, 44, 44, 47, 53, 52, 52, 51, 52, 40… $ race White, White, White, White, White, White, White, White, White,… $ rincome $8000 to 9999, $8000 to 9999, Not applicable, Not applicable, … $ partyid "Ind,near rep", "Not str republican", "Independent", "Ind,near… $ relig Protestant, Protestant, Protestant, Orthodox-christian, None, … $ denom "Southern baptist", "Baptist-dk which", "No denomination", "No… $ tvhours 12, NA, 2, 4, 1, NA, 3, NA, 0, 3, 2, NA, 1, NA, 1, 7, NA, 3, 3… ``` ::: ::: ## Order by Appearance ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *Can I order my levels by which appear first in the data?* ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} gss_cat |> mutate( marital = fct_inorder(marital) ) |> ggplot(aes(y = marital)) + geom_bar() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## Order by Frequency ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *How can I order my levels by their number of observations?* ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} gss_cat |> mutate( marital = fct_infreq(marital) ) |> ggplot(aes(y = marital)) + geom_bar() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## Reversing Order ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *Can I quickly reverse the order of my factors?* ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} gss_cat |> mutate( marital = marital |> fct_infreq() |> fct_rev() ) |> ggplot(aes(y = marital)) + geom_bar() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## Creating a Summary Table ::: {.fs80} Let's calculate the average age for each marital status group to play with. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gss_age <- gss_cat |> drop_na(age) |> summarize( .by = marital, mean_age = mean(age) ) |> print() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 2 marital mean_age 1 Never married 33.9 2 Divorced 51.1 3 Widowed 71.7 4 Married 48.7 5 Separated 45.3 6 No answer 52.4 ``` ::: ::: ## Order by Value ::: {.fs80} Order by another variable in the dataset ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} # Order by average age gss_age |> mutate( marital = fct_reorder( marital, # factor to reorder mean_age # values to order by ) ) |> ggplot( aes( x = mean_age, y = marital ) ) + geom_col() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## Manual Reordering ::: {.fs80} Manually bring one or more variables to the front / bottom ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} gss_age |> mutate( marital = fct_relevel( marital, "No answer", # first "Divorced" # second ) ) |> ggplot(aes( x = mean_age, y = marital )) + geom_col() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: # Modifying Levels ## Why Modify Levels? ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="60%"} - Sometimes the data you inherit has messy categories - You might need to combine small, specific groups into larger, more general ones for analysis - Categorical variables with too many levels can cause issues - Modifying levels allows us to tidy up before plotting or modeling ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv4 width="40%"} {{< lif "../../icons/tools.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ::: ## Recoding Levels ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *How do we rename levels to make them clearer?* ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} gss_cat |> mutate(partyid = fct_recode(partyid, "rep, strong" = "Strong republican", "rep, weak" = "Not str republican", "ind, rep" = "Ind,near rep", "ind" = "Independent", "ind, dem" = "Ind,near dem", "dem, weak" = "Not str democrat", "dem, strong" = "Strong democrat" )) |> count(partyid) |> print(n = 10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 10 × 2 partyid n 1 No answer 154 2 Don't know 1 3 Other party 393 4 rep, strong 2314 5 rep, weak 3032 6 ind, rep 1791 7 ind 4119 8 ind, dem 2499 9 dem, weak 3690 10 dem, strong 3490 ``` ::: ::: ## Collapsing Levels ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *How do we group many small categories into a few large ones?* ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gss_cat |> mutate(party_simple = fct_collapse(partyid, other = c("No answer", "Don't know", "Other party"), rep = c("Strong republican", "Not str republican"), ind = c("Ind,near rep", "Independent", "Ind,near dem"), dem = c("Not str democrat", "Strong democrat") )) |> count(party_simple, sort = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 2 party_simple n 1 ind 8409 2 dem 7180 3 rep 5346 4 other 548 ``` ::: ::: ## Many Small Groups ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gss_cat |> ggplot(aes(y = relig)) + geom_bar() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Lumping Small Groups ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *What if we only care about the most common categories?* ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gss_cat |> mutate( # Keep the 5 largest religions and lump all others relig_lumped = fct_lump_n(relig, n = 5) ) |> count(relig_lumped, sort = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 2 relig_lumped n 1 Protestant 10846 2 Catholic 5124 3 None 3523 4 Other 913 5 Christian 689 6 Jewish 388 ``` ::: ::: ## Other Ways to Lump ::: {.fs80} **Question:** *What if I want to lump based on proportions rather than a fixed count?* ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gss_cat |> mutate( # Keep religions that appear at least 5% of the time relig_prop = fct_lump_prop(relig, prop = 0.05) ) |> count(relig_prop, sort = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 2 relig_prop n 1 Protestant 10846 2 Catholic 5124 3 None 3523 4 Other 1990 ``` ::: :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
